section.title: A Refuge in Old Age
section.sectionRationale: An individual lament with no superscription, its language so closely echoes earlier Davidic prayers (compare Psalm 31, 35, 40, 70) that many read it as an old man's prayer, perhaps David near the end of his life, refusing to let fading strength silence his hope or his praise.
section.thesis: Though old age, mocking enemies, and failing strength threaten to silence hope, the aging believer clings to the God who has carried him from the womb, and resolves to keep proclaiming God's righteousness to the next generation until every ounce of strength is spent.
section.frameNote: Five movements: a cry for refuge, verses 1 to 4; a lifetime of praise recalled, verses 5 to 8; a plea not to be forsaken in old age, verses 9 to 13; undying hope that keeps proclaiming God to the next generation, verses 14 to 18; praise for God's restoring righteousness, verses 19 to 24.

verses.text: In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame.
In Your justice, rescue and deliver me; incline Your ear and save me.
Be my {{tsur|rock}} of refuge, where I can always go. Give the command to save me, for You are my rock and my fortress.
Deliver me, O my God, from the hand of the wicked, from the grasp of the unjust and ruthless.
For You are my hope, O Lord GOD, my confidence from my youth.
I have leaned on You since birth; You pulled me from my mother's womb. My praise is always for You.
I have become a portent to many, but You are my strong refuge.
My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.

units.label: Do not forsake me in old age

verses.text: Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails.
For my enemies speak against me, and those who lie in wait for my life conspire,
saying, "God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him."
Be not far from me, O God. Hurry, O my God, to help me.
May the accusers of my soul be ashamed and consumed; may those who seek my harm be covered with scorn and disgrace.

units.label: Undying hope
units.note: proclaiming God to the next generation

verses.text: But I will always {{tiqvah|hope}} and will praise You more and more.
My mouth will declare Your righteousness and Your salvation all day long, though I cannot know their full measure.
I will come in the strength of the Lord GOD; I will proclaim Your righteousness, Yours alone.
O God, You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I proclaim Your marvelous deeds.
Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation, Your might to all who are to come.
Your righteousness reaches to the heavens, O God, You who have done great things. Who, O God, is like You?
Though You have shown me many troubles and misfortunes, You will revive me once again. Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up.
You will increase my honor and comfort me once again.
So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praise to You with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel.
When I sing praise to You my lips will shout for joy, along with my soul, which You have redeemed.
My tongue will indeed proclaim Your righteousness all day long, for those who seek my harm are disgraced and confounded.

tsur.gloss: Rock, cliff, stronghold. Paired here with fortress, it pictures God as unmoving refuge, a place the psalmist can always return to no matter how old or weak he grows.

tiqvah.gloss: Hope, expectation, a cord stretched forward toward what is coming. The psalmist's hope is not wishful thinking but a forward-leaning trust that keeps producing praise, more and more, as life goes on.

basic.context: This psalm has no superscription, but its language echoes earlier prayers of David so closely that many read it as his prayer in old age, perhaps during Absalom's revolt, when the king was aged, weakened, and mocked by enemies who said God had abandoned him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the honest prayer of a believer whose body is failing and whose enemies taunt him, yet who refuses to let weakness become an excuse for silence. It models, rather than commands, how faith perseveres into old age.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist calls God his tsur, rock, an unmoving refuge, and clings to tiqvah, hope, a forward-leaning expectation rather than idle wishing. Both words anchor a life that keeps praising even as strength fails.
basic.typology: The plea to be sustained from the womb into old age and gray hairs points to Christ, who never abandons His own from infancy to the grave, and the resolve to proclaim God's might to the next generation anticipates the church's ongoing witness to Christ across every generation.
basic.christ: The enemies' taunt in verse 11, 'God has forsaken him; there is no one to rescue him,' is echoed almost word for word at the cross, 'He trusts in God. Let God rescue Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43. The psalmist's confidence that God did not, in the end, abandon him anticipates the greater truth that God did not abandon His Son to the grave.
basic.god: God is the psalmist's refuge from birth to old age, a rock who does not withdraw when strength fails, and who revives His people even from the depths of the earth.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 27:43 echoes the very taunt of verse 11 against Jesus at the cross. Isaiah 46:3-4 promises God will carry His people to old age and gray hairs. 2 Timothy 4:16-18 shows Paul, near the end of his life, rescued and still proclaiming.
basic.oneStory: This lament of an aging believer's undying hope threads into the whole Bible's story of God's unbroken faithfulness from birth to death, fulfilled in Christ, who was mocked with these very words yet was not abandoned by the Father, guaranteeing that all who take refuge in Him will be carried through to glory.

context.literary:
Psalm 71 is a long prayer of twenty-four verses that circles rather than marches. It returns three times to the same ground, in three waves. The first wave, verses 1 to 8, moves from refuge to a lifelong testimony. The second, verses 9 to 16, turns on old age and the enemy's taunt and ends in resolve. The third, verses 17 to 24, looks back to youth, forward to the next generation and finally to full-throated praise. Each wave begins in fear and ends in praise, so the psalm teaches by demonstration that lament and hope belong in one prayer.

The psalm is stitched from other prayers. Verses 1 to 3 are nearly Psalm 31:1 to 3, the plea in verse 12 is borrowed from Psalm 70, the confession of trust from the womb in verse 6 echoes Psalm 22:9 and 22:10, and the wish that enemies be ashamed in verse 13 echoes Psalm 35:26. The old man does not invent a new vocabulary. He prays with the words he has known all his life, which is one of the psalm's quiet points: the words that carried him in youth are the ones he takes into age.

Small repeated words hold the design together. 'Righteousness' comes five times, in verses 2, 15, 16, 19 and 24, and the word BSB renders 'justice' in verse 2 is the same word. 'All day long' recurs in verses 8, 15 and 24, and 'always' in verses 3, 6 and 14. The opening plea, 'let me never be put to shame,' verse 1, is answered by the closing report that those who seek his harm are 'disgraced and confounded,' verse 24. The psalm ends where its first line asked it to.

A second thread is the verb 'forsake.' The enemy says 'God has forsaken him,' verse 11, and the psalmist answers by praying the very same verb back in verses 9 and 18, 'do not forsake me.' He takes the taunt and turns it into a petition. The enemy's claim is treated as a lie to be prayed against, not a fact to be believed.
context.historical:
The psalm carries no title, which is rare in this part of the Psalter, and it therefore invites two readings that need not exclude each other. One reads it as David's prayer in his last years, and the setting most often proposed is Absalom's revolt, when the king fled Jerusalem weeping with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:30. Ahithophel had defected, 2 Samuel 15:31, and Shimei threw stones and curses, 2 Samuel 16:5 to 8, declaring that the LORD had handed the kingdom to Absalom. Psalm 3, which the Psalter ties to the same flight, records the same sneer in the words 'Many say of me, God will not deliver him,' Psalm 3:2. Psalm 71:11, 'God has forsaken him,' sounds like the same voice.

The other reading takes the psalm as a prayer for the aged in Israel generally. David himself was old and frail at the end, 1 Kings 1:1, and the Psalter sits beside a world in which age was not simply a stage of life but a threat. An elderly man with no strong sons and no land could be pushed to the margins, and an old ruler could be pushed off his throne. To be 'discarded' in old age, verse 9, was a real possibility. The Torah answers it with honor for the gray head, Leviticus 19:32, and Proverbs calls gray hair a crown of glory, Proverbs 16:31.

The testimony language of the psalm belongs to Israel's culture of remembrance. Parents were to tell their children the works of the LORD, and the Psalter itself commits each generation to declaring them to the next, Psalm 78:4 to 7 and Psalm 145:4. The old man of Psalm 71 asks to be kept alive for this task: 'until I proclaim Your power to the next generation,' verse 18. He is not asking for years for their own sake but for the sake of those who will hear.

The harp and the lyre in verse 22 place the closing praise in the temple orchestra, and the title 'the Holy One of Israel' belongs to the vocabulary of Isaiah and the Psalter, appearing again in Psalm 78:41 and 89:18. The psalm's pledge is public: the man will sing it where people can hear.
context.canonical:
Psalm 71 is the Bible's most extended prayer about growing old, and it gathers threads from across the canon. God had promised His people through Isaiah, 'Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray,' Isaiah 46:4. The psalm asks for exactly this, in nearly the same words, verse 18, and the reader hears the promise and the prayer answering each other. Psalm 92:14 says the righteous 'will still bear fruit' in old age, and Psalm 71 is a picture of what that fruit is: testimony.

It sits just before Psalm 72, and the pairing is deliberate to anyone who reads on. Psalm 71 ends with an old man asking to speak of God's might to the next generation, and Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king's son. The generational hand-off in the one psalm becomes the actual hand-off in the next. The note at the end of Psalm 72, 'the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended,' then closes Book II on an old king who has done what Psalm 71 asked.

The complaint about being forsaken links to Psalm 22, whose first line 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' Jesus prays from the cross, Matthew 27:46. Psalm 71 turns the same verb into a plea that it not happen. Hebrews 13:5 gives the New Testament reply for every believer: 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.'

Paul's last letter reads like a commentary on the psalm. 'At my first defense, no one stood with me,' he writes, 'But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed,' 2 Timothy 4:16 and 17. He expects to be 'delivered from the mouth of the lion' and rescued from every evil action, verses 17 and 18. The old apostle asks to go on proclaiming to the end, and God grants it. He also tells Timothy to continue in what he has learned, since he has known the Holy Scriptures 'from infancy,' 2 Timothy 3:14 and 15, and remembers the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother and mother, 2 Timothy 1:5. That is Psalm 71:17 and 18 lived out across three generations.

Paul also gives the New Testament's summary of the psalm's hope when he says that although our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day, 2 Corinthians 4:16. The psalm's 'revive me once again,' verse 20, is a promise of exactly this, and it finds its end in resurrection.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written for those who have never doubted God and are now afraid that God will stop. Its author wanted the elderly, the weakened and the mocked to know that they had a right to pray this prayer, and that it was not disloyal to say so. The plea 'do not discard me' is not an accusation. It is the honest voice of someone who has spent a lifetime believing in God's faithfulness and now sees the body failing.

The author also wanted young readers to learn from the old. The whole psalm is a testimony passed to the next generation. It tells a listener that God has been the man's teacher from youth, verse 17, that he has been carried since birth, verse 6, and that he plans to go on speaking until his last breath. A younger reader learns that faithfulness is long, that it survives fear, and that the God who was trusted at twenty can be trusted at eighty.

A third intention concerns the enemy's voice. The taunt of verse 11 says that suffering proves abandonment: if God were with him, this would not be happening. The psalm exposes that reasoning as false. He answers by naming his lifelong evidence and by refusing to conclude that trouble means God has left. That answer is as needed now as when the psalm was first prayed.

Finally, the author wanted the psalm to end well. It does not resolve every problem, but it ends with the harp, the lyre and a soul that has been redeemed, verses 22 and 23. Hope, in this psalm, is not a mood but an intention to praise: 'I will always hope and will praise You more and more.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one person's fear and his enemies' cruelty. It does not tell us that everyone who ages will be attacked, or that old age is a curse. Nor does it say that faithful believers will never be weak, sick or discarded by the world. It says the opposite: the psalmist's strength does fail, verse 9, and troubles do come, verse 20. What he is promised is not immunity but company.

What the psalm prescribes is a way of holding age. Pray the whole of your fear out loud, including the thing you dread most. Rehearse what God has done since your youth. Refuse to accept the world's verdict that weakness means abandonment. And keep a purpose: to declare God's righteousness and power to those who come after. Elders in the church are not to be treated as spent forces but as the bearers of the testimony, and younger members are not to leave them to pray alone.

There is also a caution about the imprecation in verse 13. The wish that the 'accusers' be consumed and covered with scorn is a request addressed to God. It is not a licence for believers to shame those who oppose them. The New Testament asks us to bless those who persecute us, Romans 12:14, and to pray that God will deal with opposition in His own way and time.

debates.question: Is this psalm David's own prayer in old age, or a later composition made for any aging worshiper?

views.label: A genuine prayer of David in his later years
views.case: The lifelong trust, the taunt that God had forsaken him, and the resemblance to Psalm 3 and the flight from Absalom fit David's experience, and the placement beside Psalm 70 and 72 keeps it inside the Davidic collection.

views.label: An anonymous prayer for the aged in Israel
views.case: The absence of a superscription is unusual in Book II, and the psalm borrows heavily from Psalms 22, 31, 35 and 70, which reads like a later worshiper drawing on inherited prayers rather than one man's occasional composition.

debates.bearing: Either way the psalm was preserved as Scripture for every believer who ages. Its authorship affects how we picture the setting, not what it asks us to do.

debates.question: What does verse 20 promise when it says God will 'bring me back up' from the depths of the earth?

views.label: Rescue from mortal danger in this life
views.case: 'Depths of the earth' is poetic language for the grave-like pit of extreme trouble, as in Psalm 63:9 and Jonah 2:6, where being brought up means being spared from death. Psalm 118:17 and 18 has the same shape, 'I will not die, but I will live.'

views.label: A hope that reaches to resurrection
views.case: The Old Testament often speaks of the pit and the grave in the same terms, and the promise that God will revive a man 'once again' from the depths of the earth can carry more than the poet may have fully seen. Christians read it in the light of Christ, who was brought up from the earth, Ephesians 4:9 and Acts 2:24.

debates.bearing: The first view keeps the psalm tied to its context and the second follows the way the canon opens out. A reader can hold both: God rescued the psalmist from a real death-like danger, and that pattern reaches its complete form in resurrection.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's opening verb, chasah, means to take shelter. Verse 1 says 'I have taken refuge' in the perfect tense, a settled fact, and then asks that he never be put to shame. The verb for shame is the ordinary bosh, and it comes back in verse 13, 'ashamed,' and in verse 24, 'disgraced,' so one root frames the whole prayer from the first plea to the last report. The rock imagery in verse 3 doubles: God is a rock of refuge and a fortress, and the second word is a different noun, metsudah, a stronghold on high ground, the kind of place David sheltered when hunted, 1 Samuel 22:4 and 5.

The word BSB renders 'confidence' in verse 5 is mivtach, from the root batach, to trust. Alongside tiqvah, hope, it names two sides of the same trust: hope looks forward, confidence rests on what has already held. The pair is explicitly tied to the psalmist's youth, or n'urim, the years of a young man.

Verse 7 has 'portent,' mofet, a sign or wonder. In Israel's vocabulary the word usually means a striking event pointing beyond itself, as with the wonders in Egypt. Here the man has become a portent, a sight people point at. His suffering is read as a sign, and the psalm insists that he is a sign of something else, God's strong refuge.

Verses 9, 11 and 18 share one verb. The psalmist prays 'do not forsake me' in verses 9 and 18, and the enemies say 'God has forsaken him' in verse 11. The verb azav is the same one that opens Psalm 22:1, 'Why have You forsaken me?' The repetition binds three moments: the enemy's claim, the psalmist's refusal and the cry of the crucified.

Verse 9's 'do not discard me' uses shalak, to throw or cast away, the word of Psalm 51:11, 'Cast me not away from Your presence.' Aging is pictured as being thrown out, and in verse 9 the phrase for old age, ziqnah, is followed by 'gray hairs' in verse 18, the same pairing that appears in Isaiah 46:4.

In verse 13 the 'accusers' of my soul come from the root satan, to accuse or oppose, the root from which the name Satan comes. The same verb appears in Psalm 109:4, 'they accuse me,' and the noun in Psalm 109:6. The psalmist's enemies play the accuser's role, and his prayer is that the accusation fails.

In verse 20 the 'depths of the earth' are tehomot, the plural of tehom, the deep. It is the same word as the deep of Genesis 1:2. The psalmist's danger is the primeval chaos, and God's revival is described as being brought up out of it.

Verse 22 calls God 'the Holy One of Israel,' qedosh Yisrael, a title common in Isaiah and found only a few times in the Psalter, including Psalm 78:41 and 89:18. The last verses use 'redeemed,' padah, for the soul, in verse 23: it is the language of ransom.

typology.type: The taunt 'God has forsaken him,' verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The enemy's charge against the righteous sufferer was spoken again at Golgotha. The chief priests and elders mocked Jesus: 'He trusts in God,' Matthew 27:43. The mockers used the logic of Psalm 71:11, that visible suffering proves divine abandonment. In Christ the correspondence deepens, because Jesus cried out 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46. Where the psalmist prays against abandonment, Christ endures it for the sake of those who will never be abandoned. The type falls short because the psalmist was never truly forsaken; Christ was.

typology.type: Brought up from the depths of the earth, verse 20
typology.fulfillment: The promise that God will revive the man and bring him back up from the depths of the earth becomes, in the light of Easter, a picture of resurrection. Jesus spoke of being three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40, and Peter announces that God raised Him, 'releasing Him from the agony of death,' Acts 2:24. The psalmist was revived within life, while Christ was raised out of death itself. The correspondence is one of pattern and not of prediction, and it opens the way for all who trust Him to be brought up in the same way.

The psalmist calls God his rock of refuge and fortress. Paul says of Israel in the wilderness that they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, 'and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The one who was Israel's refuge is the same Person who came in flesh and now shelters believers. The New Testament does not say every mention of a rock refers to Christ, and the type here rests on Paul's own use. It also falls short in that the psalmist's rock was a name for God's steadiness, while in Christ the Rock is a Person who suffered, died and rose.

typology.type: Telling the next generation, verses 17 and 18
typology.fulfillment: The old man asks to keep speaking of God's power to those who come after. The pattern runs on into the church, where Paul urges Timothy to continue in what he learned from infancy, 2 Timothy 3:14 and 15, and Anna, well along in years, speaks of the Child to all who are waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem, Luke 2:36 to 38. The commission that David's psalm sets in the Psalter is taken up in the Great Commission. The type falls short because Israel's telling passed on the memory of what God had done, while the church proclaims the One in whom that work is complete.

study.christ:
The clearest link between Psalm 71 and Christ is the taunt in verse 11. 'God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him.' The words of the enemies in the psalm are the words of the enemies of Jesus. On the night of His arrest a crowd came out with swords and clubs to seize Him, and at the cross the chief priests, scribes and elders jeered that God should deliver Him if He wanted Him, Matthew 27:43. The scene in Matthew 27:39 to 44 has the same shape as Psalm 71:10 and 11: the suffering of the righteous is read as the sign of God's absence. The gospel takes the psalm's fear and shows it happening, in its fullest form, to the only Person who did not deserve it.

The difference is decisive. The psalmist prays 'do not forsake me,' and God does not. Jesus prays from the cross, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46, and in that hour He bore what the psalm dreads. He took the place of the abandoned so that no believer will ever have to hear God say 'I have left you.' The promise that God will not leave or forsake His people, Hebrews 13:5, is founded on this.

Verse 20 points to Christ as the promise of resurrection. The psalmist says that God will revive him 'even from the depths of the earth.' In the psalm this is a rescue within the horizon of an old man's life, but the New Testament speaks of Christ's death in the same landscape. He descended to the lower parts of the earth and ascended above all the heavens, Ephesians 4:9 and 10, and He was three days in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40. Peter can say that God raised Him, 'releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:24. What the psalmist hoped for in part, Christ received in full.

Verse 16 says 'I will proclaim Your righteousness, Yours alone.' This is the theme of the gospel. Paul writes that 'the righteousness of God has been revealed,' and comes 'through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe,' Romans 3:21 and 22. The old man who says his own righteousness is worthless and God's is everything is speaking the language of justification by grace. Christ is the place where God's righteousness is shown, and He is called by Peter 'the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, echoing the psalm's 'Holy One of Israel,' verse 22.

There is also a link through the theme of a lifelong dependence, from the womb. Isaiah's servant says 'The LORD called Me from the womb,' Isaiah 49:1, and the whole of Jesus' life was lived in dependence on the Father, John 5:19. The Christ who trusted from the womb and the believer who trusts from youth stand in one line.

A caution: this is not a prediction of Jesus' life in every detail. The psalm speaks of old age and Jesus died in His thirties, so the connection is by theme, by taunt and by the pattern of the righteous sufferer, not by biography.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 71 is a God with a long memory of one person. The psalmist has known Him since before he could think: 'I have leaned on You since birth; You pulled me from my mother's womb,' verse 6. That is a doctrine of providence in its most personal form. God does not begin caring for people at some point in their lives. He was there at birth, in youth, in strength and now in weakness, and the psalm assumes that His care is continuous.

He is a God whose righteousness is the ground of hope. The word 'righteousness' comes five times in the psalm, and each time it is God's righteousness, not the man's. It is a righteousness that acts, that rescues, delivers and saves, verse 2, and one that 'reaches to the heavens,' verse 19. The man appeals to it in verse 2 and promises to proclaim it 'Yours alone,' verse 16. The psalm depicts God's justice not as cold accounting but as the energy by which He puts things right for the weak.

He is a God who does not need the man's strength. The psalmist says he will come 'in the strength of the Lord GOD,' verse 16, and that is the whole point of ending the psalm where it does. His body fails, and God is unaffected. The phrase 'Who, O God, is like You?', verse 19, echoes the song at the sea, Exodus 15:11, and it puts the question of comparison at the centre of the psalm. No power, no age, no enemy, no grave is on the same scale as the God who has done great things.

He is honest about suffering. The psalm says God 'showed' the man many troubles and misfortunes, verse 20. It does not hide that God permits and even uses trouble. It also says God 'will revive me once again,' which holds together sovereignty over the trouble and mercy in it. The God who allows the pit is the God who lifts out of the pit.

He is the Holy One of Israel, verse 22. His nearness does not lower His holiness, and His holiness does not put Him beyond reach. The man calls Him at once his rock, his fortress, his God and the Holy One. These are the words of intimacy and awe together.

For worship the psalm shapes several habits. It asks us to tell our story back to God, to tell it to others and to keep telling it as strength ebbs. It asks us to see that faithfulness is not a burst of feeling but a lifelong reliance, and that God's care for the old is as real as His care for the young. And it asks us to meet the taunt 'God has abandoned him' with the plain reply of a life that has been carried. The psalm sees no contradiction in a God who is both far above all and near enough to be leaned on from the womb.

crossReferences.note: The opening verses of Psalm 71 are almost a quotation. Psalm 31 is a lament of David in trouble that ends in trust, and Psalm 71 takes over its first three verses about refuge, rock and fortress. The borrowing shows an old man praying the psalms he learned in youth.

David says that God brought him from the womb and that he was cast upon God from birth. Psalm 71:6 makes the same confession of lifelong dependence. Psalm 22 also opens with the cry 'Why have You forsaken me?', the same verb that Psalm 71 uses in the enemies' taunt and in the plea against being forsaken.

Written, according to its title, when David fled from Absalom, this psalm records the sneer 'God will not deliver him.' It is very close to Psalm 71:11, and it supports the view that the taunt belongs to the flight from Jerusalem, whether or not Psalm 71 was written then.

God tells Israel that He has carried them from the womb and will bear them up when they turn gray. The promise is the divine answer to the prayer of Psalm 71:9 and 18. God commits Himself in advance to what the old man asks.

The righteous flourish like a palm and a cedar, and in old age they still bear fruit, proclaiming that the LORD is upright. Psalm 92 gives the positive picture of what Psalm 71 desires, an old age that goes on bearing the fruit of testimony.

The people commit themselves to declaring God's praises and might to the next generation, so that the coming generation would know them and put their confidence in God. It is the corporate version of Psalm 71:18, and it shows why the old man's request has such weight.

Psalm 71:12 quotes the urgent prayer of Psalm 70. Here we see the earlier short cry taken into a longer prayer. The neighbor psalms belong together, one an emergency flare and the other a whole life brought to God.

The mockers at the cross speak the words of Psalm 71:11, and Jesus prays the words of Psalm 22:1. Here the taunt and the forsakenness of the psalm meet in one scene. The righteous man is treated as abandoned, and in the case of Jesus, on behalf of others, He truly was.

The writer quotes God's promise 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.' It is the New Testament's answer to the psalm's plea 'do not forsake me,' and it grounds the answer in a promise that cannot fail.

Paul, near the end of his life, was deserted at his first defense but was strengthened by the Lord and rescued from the lion's mouth. His words echo the psalm's confidence that God stands by the aged and lets them finish their testimony.

Paul writes that although the outer self is wasting away, the inner self is renewed day by day. It reads like a summary of Psalm 71: strength fails, yet the man is revived and goes on praising, and the source is God.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 71 belongs to the part of the Bible's story that asks what God does with His people over time. The story begins with a creation in which humanity was made to live in the presence of God. Death entered, and with it the slow failure of the body, the greying of hair and the loss of strength that the psalm records. Old age in this psalm is therefore not just a private experience but a sign of the world after Genesis 3. The psalmist feels the decline of a fallen creation in his own bones.

Against that decline the Bible sets God's word about carrying His people. He tells Israel through Isaiah that He has carried them from birth and will carry them to old age, Isaiah 46:4. The Exodus is the pattern: God brought a people out of slavery and carried them, as a man carries his son, through the wilderness, Deuteronomy 1:31. Psalm 71 takes that national memory and puts it in a single life. What God did for the nation, He does for the individual.

The psalm then looks forward. The old man wants to keep proclaiming until a new generation has heard, verse 18, and Psalm 72 immediately shows a king's son being prayed over. The same relay runs through Scripture: Abraham to Isaac, Moses to Joshua, David to Solomon, Elijah to Elisha, Paul to Timothy. No one holds the testimony for good, and every faithful life is a handing over. In this way the psalm is part of the answer to how the story continues after each person's strength runs out.

The story reaches its center in Christ, who was mocked with the words of verse 11 and truly forsaken so that no one who trusts Him will be. He went down into the deep and was brought up again, and His resurrection is the first-fruits of the revival the psalmist hoped for, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The church now lives in the time between that rising and its completion, and Paul describes it in terms very like the psalm: outward wasting, inward renewal, 2 Corinthians 4:16.

The story ends in a new creation where the losses of age are undone. God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The one who prayed 'do not discard me in my old age' is answered with a city where nothing wears out and no one is discarded, where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The psalmist's promise of more honor and comfort, verse 21, is fulfilled there, and the harp and the lyre are picked up again.

sermon.title: Seven Resolutions for Finishing Well
sermon.why: Preached from Psalm 71 at a funeral, Piper draws seven resolutions for aging and dying well straight from this psalm's own language of refuge, remembered grace, undying hope, and praise that refuses to grow quiet.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God not to do as he grows old?

options.text: Discard him in his old age or forsake him when his strength fails, verse 9.
options.note: This is the psalm's central plea, repeated again in verse 18.

options.text: Give him more wealth in his later years.
options.note: The psalm is not concerned with wealth but with God's continued presence.

options.text: Remove all his enemies immediately.
options.note: He does ask for rescue from enemies, but the central plea concerns being forsaken in old age.

options.text: Let him die quickly and painlessly.
options.note: The psalm never asks for a quick death; it asks to keep proclaiming God as long as life lasts.

quiz.q: What do the psalmist's enemies say about him, according to verse 11?

options.text: "God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him."
options.note: This taunt is later echoed almost word for word against Jesus at the cross.

options.text: "He has always been faithful; leave him in peace."
options.note: This is the opposite of the enemies' mocking taunt.

options.text: "He is too powerful to be defeated."
options.note: The enemies mock his apparent weakness and abandonment, not his power.

options.text: "His God has never existed."
options.note: Close in spirit but not the actual wording; they claim God has abandoned him, not that God does not exist.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist resolve to do even in old age and gray hairs, verse 18?

options.text: Proclaim God's power and might to the next generation and to all who are to come.
options.note: This is his explicit resolve, the reason he asks not to be forsaken yet.

options.text: Retire from all worship and public life.
options.note: The opposite; he insists on continuing to proclaim God's works.

options.text: Seek comfort only in his family's wealth.
options.note: His comfort is in declaring God's works, not accumulated wealth.

options.text: Wait silently for death without speaking further.
options.note: He explicitly resolves to keep speaking, not to fall silent.

quiz.q: What confidence does the psalmist express about restoration in verses 20-21?

options.text: That God will revive him again and bring him back up even from the depths of the earth.
options.note: Despite many troubles, he trusts God to restore and honor him again.

options.text: That he will never face any more trouble again.
options.note: He acknowledges troubles have come and may come; his hope is in God's revival, not the absence of trouble.

options.text: That his enemies will become his friends.
options.note: The psalm expects the enemies to be disgraced, not befriended.

options.text: That his physical strength will never fail.
options.note: He already acknowledges his strength is failing; his hope is in God's power, not unfailing physical strength.

quiz.q: How does this psalm connect most directly to the New Testament?

options.text: The taunt of verse 11 is echoed almost word for word against Jesus at the cross, Matthew 27:43.
options.note: This is the psalm's most striking and direct New Testament connection.

options.text: It predicts the exact number of years Jesus would live.
options.note: The psalm makes no such prediction.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The connection to the cross's taunt is a direct and striking one.

options.text: It describes a miracle Jesus later performed.
options.note: The psalm is a prayer, not an account of a miracle, though its language of revival anticipates resurrection hope.

questions: The psalmist has leaned on God since birth, verse 6. Where can you trace God's faithfulness across your own life, from childhood until now?
He fears being forsaken specifically in old age and weakness, verse 9. What losses of strength, health, or usefulness make you most afraid that God might let you go?
The enemies' taunt in verse 11 is echoed against Jesus Himself at the cross. How does knowing that Christ bore this very mockery change how you face your own seasons of feeling forsaken?
The psalmist resolves to keep proclaiming God's works to the next generation even in old age, verse 18. Who is in your life that needs to hear what God has done for you?
Despite many troubles, verse 20, he trusts God to revive him again. Where do you need that same confidence today, that God can still bring you back up from a low place?

translationNotes.note: Rock and fortress translate two related Hebrew military terms for a stronghold; paired together they intensify the picture of an unmoving refuge the psalmist can always run to.

The Hebrew verb behind 'pulled me' is somewhat unusual, and some render it 'you are my support' from birth rather than 'you pulled me forth'; either way the verse affirms God's care from the very beginning of life.

The title 'Lord GOD' renders the divine name paired with a title of sovereignty, used twice in this psalm, verses 5 and 16, underscoring that the psalmist's hope rests in God's supreme authority, not his own strength.
